doc_summary: Marks argues interpretability researchers should validate their insights by demonstrating downstream applications, even toy ones, that beat the best non-interp baselines in a fair fight. He argues this guards against illusory and unimportant insights.

items.claim: Prefers evidence that an insight lets you do something no one else can (beating baselines on a downstream task) over compelling-looking qualitative results because illusory insights break down when you try to use them.
items.quote: I think that if your insights allow you to do something that no one else is able to do—i.e. to outperform baselines on a downstream task—then they're less likely to be illusory or unimportant.

items.claim: Distrusts results that look intuitively compelling but have not been checked against a trivial control, since saliency maps looked convincing yet matched what a random network produced.
items.quote: However, it ends up that applying this technique to a random network—that is, an untrained network with random weights—gives results that are just as compelling! This suggests that saliency maps were just functioning as something like "simple edge detectors,"

items.claim: Insists on beating the best baseline that exists, not just the best one you know of, and stays suspicious of a method until a task is exhibited where the simple baseline fails and the method succeeds.
items.quote: I'll worry that SHIFT is "fancy token deletion" until someone exhibits a task where token deletion fails but SHIFT succeeds.

items.claim: Prefers fair-fight comparisons with explicitly specified affordances over unconstrained comparisons because they capture most of the validation benefit while keeping the test well-defined.
items.quote:
Clearly specify which affordances are allowed (e.g. in which ways are you allowed to interact with the model? what data are you allowed to use?)
Test the best techniques for accomplishing the task that make use of the same affordances.

items.claim: Prefers toy downstream tasks whose goal does not reference the method over self-referential goals like finding a circuit, because only the former can validate that insights matter.
items.quote: By **downstream application** I mean a task with a goal that *does not itself make reference to interpretability*. E.g. "Make [model] more honest" is a downstream application.

items.claim: Warns that validation methodology lags behind new kinds of claims, since ablations and sanity checks are developed post-hoc, and proposes downstream tasks to side-step that lag.
items.quote: These days, we know that we should do various ablations (e.g. random network ablations) to tests for these types of illusions. But our ablations aren't exhaustive, and were largely developed post-hoc in order to validate new types of claims.

items.claim: Treats whether toy-task problems occur naturally as a question that can be partly handled by conceptual forecasting, so does not demand in-the-wild realism before a demo counts as useful.
items.quote: With "no holds barred" and "in the wild" demos, you start to get into questions of whether the problems that you're able to solve are problems which are likely to naturally occur; while these questions are ultimately empirical, I think they can partly be substituted by conceptual arguments

items.claim: Separates true-but-unimportant insights from important ones, judging an insight by whether it could plausibly matter for anything you would do.
items.quote: The observation you made is *true* (and perhaps, to some people, *interesting*) but not *important*—what are you going to *do* with it?
